prime.problem: A window median needs the middle of k values, which neither a Counter nor a monotonic deque keeps. Sorting every window is O(n · k log k), about 10⁹ comparisons for n = 10⁵, k = 10³, and a sorted list with insort shifts O(k) per step.
prime.fits: Comes right after the heaps card, because it is two heaps working together plus heapq's lazy deletion. It reuses the fixed-window sweep from the monotonic deque card; the difference is that no value can be thrown away for good.
expect: lo: a max-heap (negated) of the low half
hi: a min-heap of the high half
median from one or both tops
lazy deletion with a gone counter
a balance number that decides one move per step
prime.goal: Report every window median in O(n log n) with the standard library only, explain why deleting lazily is safe, and say when buried entries make the heaps grow toward n.

attend: Why does splitting into a low half and a high half put the median on a heap top?
Why is lo allowed to hold one extra value when k is odd?
What does the balance number count, and why is one move always enough to fix it?
Why is it safe to delete a leaving value by value rather than by its index?
When can a buried value stay in a heap until the very end?

must: Every value in lo ≤ every value in hi, with sizes (k + 1) // 2 and k // 2 → the median is top(lo) for odd k, or the mean of both tops for even k → reading it is O(1)
A heap can only remove its top cheaply → when a value leaves, record gone[v] += 1 and remove it only when it surfaces on a top → each value is pruned at most once → O(log n) per step
The leaver and the newcomer each shift the real size difference by ±1 → balance is −2, 0 or +2 → at most one top moves across → the halves stay the right sizes

Buried leavers are never removed early → values far from the median never reach a top (on rising input all 20 of range(20) stay, 17 stale; on n = 10⁵ random values with k = 1,000 the heaps peak at 91,491 entries) → heaps grow toward n, not k → O(n log n) time and O(n) space
elevated: Equal values are interchangeable → deleting any copy of 3 leaves the same two halves → so lazy deletion by value is correct even with duplicates
reference: the source's C++ multiset with a middle iterator (and its missing brace)
the bisect baseline in the code file

compress.prompt: From memory, draw lo and hi for the window [−3, 5, 3] and explain in 3–5 sentences how one step works: which value leaves, where the newcomer goes, how balance is fixed and when stale values are removed.
checklist: lo (max-heap) holds the low half plus the extra for odd k; hi holds the high half
the median is top(lo) for odd k
gone[leaver] += 1; its side decides balance −1 or +1
the newcomer goes to lo if ≤ top(lo), else hi; one top moves if balance is ±2
prune stale tops from both heaps; buried stale values wait

retrieve.q: Explain why the two-heap split makes the median O(1) to read but O(log k) to maintain.
answer: the median is always at the boundary between the halves, which is where the tops are
each step pushes, possibly moves one top and pops stale tops, each O(log size)

retrieve.q: Walk through step i = 5 of the trace (window [−3, 5, 3], −1 leaving, 3 arriving).
answer: 3 > top(lo) = −1, so it goes into hi: balance −2
lo is one short: move hi's min 3 into lo
−1 is buried under 3 in lo and stays; the median is 3

retrieve.q: Your input is a sorted stream of sensor readings. What happens to memory with two heaps, and what would you use instead?
answer: on monotone input the leavers sit at the bottom of their heap and never surface
so the heaps hold every value seen: O(n) memory, not O(k)
a SortedList (add, remove, index k // 2) holds exactly k values
an order-statistic Fenwick tree over value ranks also stays at the number of distinct values

compare.q: Both slide a window of k. Why can the deque forget values forever while the median must keep every value until it leaves?
answer: a smaller, older value can never become the max, so the deque discards it
any value can become the median as others leave
so the median keeps all k values (plus buried ones) in two heaps
cost: O(1) amortized per step for the max, O(log n) for the median

compare.q: The heaps card uses one heap for smallest next; this card uses two for the middle. What does the second heap buy, and what new bookkeeping does it bring?
answer: one heap exposes only one extreme
two heaps facing each other expose both sides of the boundary, where the median lives
they must be kept the right sizes (balance) and consistent (lo ≤ hi)
lazy deletion must track which side a leaver was on

predict.q: Run the two-heap median on range(20) with k = 3. Before running: how many entries do the two heaps hold together at the end, and how many of them are stale?
predict.answer: 20 entries, 17 stale. On a rising input each leaver is the smallest value in lo, which sits at the bottom of a max-heap, while every newcomer lands on top; the leavers never surface, so nothing is ever pruned. Only the 3 values of the last window are real.

apply.task: Run median_sliding_window on [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3, 6, 7] with k = 4, printing lo, hi and gone after each step. Then add a counter for the total heap size and run it on range(20) with k = 3.
apply.done: The medians are [0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 4.0, 5.5], every median is the mean of the two tops, and the range(20) run ends with 20 entries in the heaps, 3 of them real.
apply.hint: For even k, lo and hi each keep k / 2 real values.
